Clinical Reference · Gastroenterology

Peptic Ulcer Disease

On this page
A mucosal break ≥5 mm penetrating the muscularis mucosae in the acid-exposed gut (stomach or duodenum) — the end result of aggression (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) outrunning mucosal defense.
H. pylori + NSAIDs ≈ 90% of cases Alarm feature → prompt EGD Bleeding PUD: ~2–10% mortality Anchor: PPI + eliminate the cause DU 4× more common than GU
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

An ulcer is not "too much acid" — it is a failed truce between the acid the stomach makes and the mucosa's ability to protect itself. Two forces are always in tension:

  • Aggression — hydrochloric acid (pumped by the parietal cell), pepsin (activated below pH 4), bile salts, and the two things that break the truce: Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs.
  • Defense — an adherent mucus–bicarbonate layer, brisk mucosal blood flow, fast epithelial renewal, and the master-regulator of all three: prostaglandins (PGE₂, made by COX-1).

Acid production is the hinge. The parietal cell integrates three stimulatory signals — histamine (H₂ receptor, from ECL cells; the dominant driver), gastrin (CCK-B receptor, from antral G cells), and acetylcholine (M₃ receptor, from the vagus). All three converge on one machine: the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase — the proton pump — which trades potassium for hydrogen ions and drives luminal pH below 2. Somatostatin (D cells) is the brake. Every acid-suppressing drug is defined by where in this circuit it acts, and the pump is the final common step — which is exactly why proton-pump inhibitors are the most complete blockade.

H. pylori survives the acid bath by making urease, splitting urea into ammonia to buffer its own microenvironment (the basis of the urea breath and rapid-urease tests). Its cytotoxins (CagA, VacA) inflame the mucosa. Where it lives decides the ulcer: antral-predominant gastritis suppresses somatostatin → gastrin rises → acid rises → duodenal ulcer; corpus-predominant gastritis causes atrophy → acid falls but cancer risk rises → gastric ulcer / adenocarcinoma. NSAIDs attack the defense side: they inhibit COX-1, depleting the protective prostaglandins that maintain mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow (a systemic effect, plus direct topical injury) — which is why NSAID ulcers are often silent until they bleed.

The mucosa is a castle wall under constant acid siege. Acid is the battering ram; H. pylori and NSAIDs are sappers digging at the foundation (and NSAIDs also cut the supply line of mortar — prostaglandins). PPIs disable the battering ram at its engine (the pump), H₂ blockers cut one of its three fuel lines, misoprostol re-supplies the mortar (a prostaglandin analog), sucralfate throws a tarp over the breach, and antibiotics evict the sappers. Heal the wall and remove the sappers, or the siege simply resumes.
Acid secretion integrates three receptors onto one pump. PPIs act at the final, irreversible step — the reason they out-heal H₂ blockers.
H. pylori (curved rods) hugging the gastric epithelium on biopsy — Giemsa stain. Urease lets it survive acid; CagA/VacA drive the gastritis that unbalances acid regulation.
Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, Helicobacter Pylori, Stomach Biopsy, Giemsa Stain (5435867593).jpg (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Electron micrograph — the multiple sheathed flagella that let H. pylori burrow through mucus to the epithelial surface.
Hpylori.jpg: * Photo Credit: Janice Carr Content Providers(s): CDC/ Dr. Patricia Fields..., HelicobacterPylori2.jpg (Public domain), via Wikimedia Commons
Therapy works on both pans: suppress/removes aggression (PPI, antibiotics, stop NSAIDs) and rebuild defense (misoprostol, sucralfate, time).
Every drug in this guide maps to one arrow in the cascade above: PPI/vonoprazan = disable the pump (final step); H₂RA = block the histamine input; antacids = neutralize acid already secreted; sucralfate = physical barrier over the ulcer base; misoprostol = PGE₁ analog that replaces the prostaglandins NSAIDs deplete; bismuth = coats the ulcer + is directly bactericidal to H. pylori; antibiotics = remove the organism driving the whole process.
🗂️

Etiology & classification

What causes the ulcer (and the mechanism)

CauseShare of PUDMechanism / clue
H. pylori~40–70% (falling in the West)Urease + CagA/VacA → chronic gastritis that dysregulates acid; antral pattern → duodenal ulcer, corpus pattern → gastric ulcer/cancer.
NSAIDs / aspirin~20–30%COX-1 inhibition → prostaglandin depletion → defense loss (systemic ≫ topical). Often painless until bleeding.
H. pylori + NSAIDCommon overlapSynergistic — each independently raises risk; together multiplicative.
Idiopathic (Hp-neg, NSAID-neg)~10–20% (rising)Diagnosis of exclusion; worse prognosis, higher rebleed — confirm truly negative testing.
Hypersecretory — Zollinger-Ellison<1%Gastrinoma → relentless acid. Suspect with multiple/refractory ulcers, distal-duodenal/jejunal ulcers, diarrhea, or ulcer + hypercalcemia (MEN-1). Check fasting gastrin off PPI.
Stress-related mucosal diseaseICU settingSplanchnic hypoperfusion. Curling ulcer (burns), Cushing ulcer (CNS injury/↑ICP → vagal acid surge).
Malignancy / otherUncommonGastric adenocarcinoma or lymphoma can ulcerate; also CMV/HSV (immunocompromised), Crohn disease. Always biopsy a gastric ulcer.

Duodenal vs gastric ulcer — they behave differently

FeatureDuodenal ulcer (DU)Gastric ulcer (GU)
Relative frequency~4× more commonLess common, older patients
Classic pain2–5 h after meals & at night; relieved by food/antacid (acid hits an empty, unbuffered bulb)Worsened by eating (food → acid onto damaged mucosa); weight loss, early satiety
Acid outputNormal-to-highNormal-to-low
H. pylori prevalence~90%~70%
Malignancy riskEssentially noneMust biopsy + confirm healing on repeat EGD (8–12 wk)
Anatomy / complicationBulb: posterior → gastroduodenal artery bleed; anterior → free perforationLesser curve; incisura. Bleeding from left gastric branches

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change PUD — and what to avoid

ComorbidityHow it changes PUD / managementDrugs to avoid / caution
Coronary disease / DAPT (recent stent)The core dilemma — stopping antiplatelets risks stent thrombosis, continuing risks rebleeding. Continue aspirin where possible and resume the P2Y12 inhibitor ASAP after hemostasis. Clopidogrel + PPI: use pantoprazole (or an H₂RA).Avoid omeprazole/esomeprazole with clopidogrel (CYP2C19 → ↓ active metabolite, FDA warning); avoid reflexive platelet transfusion for reversal.
Cirrhosis / portal hypertensionBleed may be variceal or ulcer (cirrhotics get both); higher rebleed & mortality; coagulopathy + thrombocytopenia. If any chance of a variceal source, start octreotide + ceftriaxone empirically before scope. Restrictive transfusion is especially important (over-transfusion raises portal pressure).NSAIDs contraindicated (precipitate AKI/HRS & bleeding); avoid over-resuscitation.
CKD / uremiaUremic platelet dysfunction → bleeding despite a normal count; idiopathic ulcers more common. DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV transiently improves platelet function; correct anemia.Renally dose/avoid NSAIDs; dose-adjust eradication antibiotics and H₂RAs for GFR.
Anticoagulation (AF / VTE / valve)Reverse for life-threatening bleed; restart usually within days–1 week once hemostasis is secure. Mechanical valve = highest thrombotic risk → shortest interruption.Balance CHA₂DS₂-VASc vs rebleed; DOAC + antiplatelet stacks bleeding risk.
Chronic NSAID need (RA/OA)If unavoidable: lowest effective dose + PPI co-therapy, or COX-2 selective, or COX-2 + PPI in the highest risk; eradicate H. pylori first.Avoid non-selective NSAIDs without gastroprotection; caution stacking NSAID + aspirin + steroid/SSRI.
Zollinger-Ellison (gastrinoma)Suspect with refractory/multiple/post-bulbar ulcers, ulcer + diarrhea, or Hp-/NSAID-negative ulcers (± MEN-1). Diagnose with fasting gastrin off PPI + secretin test; treat with high-dose PPI + tumor workup.Don't check gastrin while on a PPI (false positive); don't miss MEN-1 screening.
Avoid / use with caution in PUD: non-selective NSAIDs & aspirin (unless indicated + gastroprotected) · NSAID + corticosteroid combinations · omeprazole/esomeprazole with clopidogrel · bisphosphonates & potassium chloride tablets (direct mucosal irritants) · ranitidine (withdrawn 2020 — NDMA) · misoprostol in pregnancy (abortifacient) · tranexamic acid for the bleeding itself (HALT-IT — no benefit, more VTE/seizures).
🩺 Clinic — outpatient optimization & prevention
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & risk

PUD usually presents as dyspepsia / epigastric pain, but the single most important point in clinic is that NSAID ulcers are frequently silent until they bleed — so "no pain" does not mean "no ulcer" in an NSAID or aspirin user. Correlate symptoms with risk factors: H. pylori exposure, NSAID/aspirin/anticoagulant use, smoking, prior ulcer, age >60.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens (mechanism)
Epigastric pain / dyspepsia70–80%Acid + pepsin on exposed sensory nerve endings in the ulcer base; gnawing/burning, often localized with one finger.
Meal-related pattern50–60%DU: pain 2–5 h post-meal & nocturnal, relieved by food/antacid (buffering). GU: pain worse with food (acid onto injured mucosa).
Nocturnal pain (wakes 12–3 am)~50% (DU)Circadian acid peak with no food to buffer it; classic for duodenal ulcer.
Nausea / bloating / belching40–55%Dysmotility & delayed gastric emptying from inflammation; non-specific.
Early satiety / anorexia25–40%Mucosal inflammation, edema; food aversion (esp. GU) → some weight loss.
Overt bleeding as first sign (melena/hematemesis)15–20%Ulcer erodes into a submucosal vessel; may be the only presentation of an NSAID ulcer.
Weight loss (unintentional)~20%Reduced intake; an alarm feature — think malignancy, refer for EGD.
Perforation (sudden severe pain + rigid abdomen)<5%Transmural erosion → free air & chemical peritonitis; anterior DU classically.
Gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting, succussion splash)<5%Chronic pyloric-channel/duodenal scarring & edema → mechanical obstruction.
The pain of PUD is a poor localizer of danger: severity of pain does not track ulcer size or bleeding risk, and up to ~40–60% of NSAID ulcers are asymptomatic. Screen by risk, not just symptoms.
ALARM features → prompt EGD (don't just empirically treat): new-onset dyspepsia age ≥60; GI bleeding / iron-deficiency anemia; unintentional weight loss; dysphagia or odynophagia; persistent vomiting; palpable mass/lymphadenopathy; family history of upper-GI cancer.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs, H. pylori testing & endoscopy

Two clinic pathways diverge on age and alarm features: patients <60 with no alarm features get non-invasive "test-and-treat" for H. pylori (ACG 2017); patients ≥60 or with any alarm feature go straight to EGD.

H. pylori urea breath test / stool antigenFirst-line active-infection test for anyone with dyspepsia <60 without alarm features, and to confirm cure later. Hold PPI ≥2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth ≥4 weeks before testing — they cause false negatives.Initial
CBCLook for iron-deficiency anemia (chronic occult blood loss) — anemia is an alarm feature that mandates EGD.Initial
Iron studies / ferritinIf microcytic anemia — confirms chronic GI blood loss and its severity.If anemic
EGD + biopsyAge ≥60 with new dyspepsia, or ANY alarm feature. Biopsy every gastric ulcer (exclude malignancy) and take antral + body biopsies for H. pylori (rapid urease test / histology).Alarm / ≥60
Fasting serum gastrinOnly if hypersecretory state suspected: multiple/refractory ulcers, distal-duodenal/jejunal ulcers, ulcer + diarrhea, or ulcer + hypercalcemia (MEN-1). Must be off PPI (PPI raises gastrin).If ZES suspected
Upright CXR / CT abdomenNOT for routine PUD — order only if perforation suspected (acute severe pain, peritonitis): free air under the diaphragm (CXR) or extraluminal air (CT, more sensitive).If perforation

Interpreting the H. pylori tests — why each can mislead you

TestDetectsWhat falsely LOWERS / raises it
Urea breath test (UBT)Active infection (urease activity)False negative: recent PPI (≤2 wk), antibiotics/bismuth (≤4 wk), active bleeding. Best test to confirm eradication.
Stool antigenActive infection (bacterial antigen)False negative: same PPI/antibiotic/bismuth washout as UBT. Cheap, good for cure testing.
Biopsy rapid urease testActive infection at endoscopyFalse negative: PPI use, recent bleeding, patchy colonization (take antrum + body). Very specific if positive.
Serology (IgG)Exposure (past OR present)Cannot confirm cure — stays positive after eradication. Largely abandoned; only a rough rule-out in high-prevalence settings.
The commonest reason a "test-and-treat" fails is a false-negative test on a patient still taking a PPI. If you cannot stop the PPI (e.g., active symptoms), a positive test still counts, but never trust a negative test done on-PPI — repeat it after a washout, or biopsy at endoscopy.
Treat

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — remove the cause, then heal

Two jobs, in this order: (1) remove the driver — eradicate H. pylori and stop NSAIDs — and (2) suppress acid to let the ulcer heal. Do only #2 and the ulcer comes back.

1
Remove the cause — eradicate H. pylori & stop NSAIDs
The single biggest determinant of cure and non-recurrence.
▾
Antibiotics remove the organism driving chronic gastritis and acid dysregulation; stopping the NSAID restores COX-1 prostaglandin defense. Eradication drops ulcer recurrence from ~60–70%/yr to <10%.

ACG 2024 shift: because U.S. clarithromycin resistance is now ~31%, empiric clarithromycin triple therapy is no longer preferred. Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days is the preferred first-line; use clarithromycin- or levofloxacin-based regimens only when susceptibility is known.

Regimen (14 days)Components & dosesWhen to pickNotes / eradication
Bismuth quadruple (preferred)PPI std-dose BID + bismuth subsalicylate 300–524 mg QID + tetracycline 500 mg QID + metronidazole 500 mg TID–QID (>1.5 g/day)First-line for essentially everyone; the go-to in penicillin allergy and after any prior macrolide.~85–90%. Overcomes clarithromycin resistance; 4 pills but robust. Warn of dark stool/tongue (bismuth).
Rifabutin triple (Talicia)Omeprazole 40 mg + amoxicillin 1000 mg + rifabutin 50 mg, every 8 h (TID) → daily omeprazole 120 / amox 3 g / rifabutin 150 mgPenicillin-tolerant patients; sidesteps clarithromycin & metronidazole resistance.~84%. Very low rifabutin resistance; check for concomitant CYP3A4 drugs.
Vonoprazan dual (Voquezna Dual Pak)Vonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1000 mg TIDPenicillin-tolerant; avoids clarithromycin/metronidazole entirely.P-CAB gives faster, stronger, food-independent acid block than PPIs → better amoxicillin efficacy.
Vonoprazan triple (Voquezna Triple Pak)Vonoprazan 20 mg + amoxicillin 1000 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg, all BIDOnly where clarithromycin susceptibility known / low local resistance.Still clarithromycin-based — same resistance caveat applies.
Clarithromycin triple / concomitantPPI BID + clarithromycin 500 BID + amoxicillin 1000 BID (± metronidazole 500 BID = concomitant)Avoid empirically — only if clarithromycin-susceptible & no prior macrolide.Historical first-line; failing due to resistance.
NSAID/aspirin driving it? Stop the NSAID if at all possible. If it must continue (e.g., high CV/rheum need): co-prescribe a PPI, switch to the lowest-dose agent, or use a COX-2 selective (celecoxib) + PPI in the highest-risk patients. Aspirin for secondary CV prevention is usually continued with a PPI, not stopped.
Salvage after failure: never reuse the same antibiotics. If clarithromycin regimen failed → bismuth quadruple or levofloxacin triple (PPI + levofloxacin 500 mg daily + amoxicillin 1000 mg BID ×14 d). If bismuth quad failed → rifabutin or levofloxacin regimen. Ideally susceptibility-guided. Always confirm eradication (see Monitoring).
2
Heal the ulcer — acid suppression (PPI)
All PPIs work; pick by interactions & cost. Duration by ulcer type.
▾
PPIs irreversibly inhibit the parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase — the final common step — holding intragastric pH >4 so mucosa can re-epithelialize (and >6 to stabilize clot during a bleed). Take 30–60 min before the first meal (they only inhibit actively secreting pumps).
PPIStartTitration → when to doubleHealing target / durationWhy pick it / caution
Omeprazole20–40 mg PO daily→ BID if refractory, high-risk, or ZESDU 4 wk · GU 8 wkPrototype; inhibits CYP2C19 → ↓ clopidogrel activation (prefer pantoprazole with clopidogrel).
Esomeprazole20–40 mg PO daily→ 40 mg BIDDU 4 wk · GU 4–8 wkS-isomer of omeprazole; potent, preferred PPI in eradication regimens.
Pantoprazole40 mg PO daily→ 40 mg BID4–8 wkLeast CYP2C19 interaction → best with clopidogrel; reliable IV form for inpatients.
Lansoprazole30 mg PO daily→ 30 mg BIDDU 4 wk · GU 8 wkOrally-disintegrating option.
Dexlansoprazole30–60 mg PO daily→ 60 mg daily4–8 wkDual delayed-release → dosing not tied to meals (flexible).
Rabeprazole20 mg PO daily→ 20 mg BIDDU 4 wk · GU 6–8 wkFast onset; minimal CYP2C19 dependence.
Famotidine (H₂RA)20–40 mg PO BID (or 40 mg qHS)Only if PPI truly not toleratedDU 6–8 wkIf PPI-intolerant. Weaker, tachyphylaxis. Ranitidine withdrawn 2020 (NDMA); avoid cimetidine (antiandrogen + CYP inhibitor).
Monitoring on PPI: for a healing course, none needed. On long-term PPI watch for hypomagnesemia, B₁₂/iron deficiency, ↑ C. difficile/pneumonia risk, fundic-gland polyps, and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping. Use the lowest effective dose and deprescribe once the cause is fixed — don't reflexively continue lifelong PPI after eradication + NSAID cessation.
3
Refractory / special situations
Non-healing ulcer, mucosal protectants, hypersecretory states.
▾

Ulcer not healed at repeat EGD? Work through the differential: non-adherence, ongoing covert NSAID/aspirin use, failed H. pylori eradication (re-test), malignancy (re-biopsy), or a hypersecretory state (Zollinger-Ellison) — check fasting gastrin off PPI.

AgentDoseRoleWhy it works / caution
Misoprostol200 mcg PO QIDNSAID-ulcer prevention/healing when NSAID must continuePGE₁ analog — directly replaces the prostaglandins NSAIDs deplete. Diarrhea/cramps limit use; contraindicated in pregnancy (abortifacient).
Sucralfate1 g PO QID (before meals + qHS)Adjunct/barrier; option in pregnancyForms a physical gel over the ulcer base. Needs acid to activate (don't co-give with PPI at the same time); binds other drugs (separate by 2 h); caution in CKD (aluminum).
High-dose PPIe.g., omeprazole 60 mg daily, titrate to acid outputZollinger-Ellison / gastrinomaHypersecretion needs profound, often BID high-dose acid blockade; refer to GI/endocrine for gastrinoma workup.
Surgery is now rare for uncomplicated PUD (medical therapy healed the field). Reserve for complications — perforation, refractory bleeding, obstruction, or malignancy — see the Wards/ICU contexts.
Monitor

Follow-up & confirm cure

📈

What to recheck, and when

ActionWhenWhy
Confirm H. pylori eradication (UBT or stool antigen)≥4 weeks after finishing antibiotics, and off PPI ≥1–2 weeksTest-of-cure is now standard for everyone treated — resistance means ~15% fail. Do not use serology (stays positive after cure).
Repeat EGD for gastric ulcers8–12 weeks after diagnosisConfirm healing and exclude gastric malignancy (re-biopsy non-healed ulcers). Duodenal ulcers do not need routine repeat EGD.
Reassess symptoms4–8 weeksPersistent symptoms despite therapy → check adherence, covert NSAID use, wrong diagnosis (functional dyspepsia, GERD), or ZES.
Deprescribe PPIOnce healed + cause removedLowest effective dose; taper to avoid rebound. Lifelong PPI only for ongoing NSAID/aspirin need, ZES, or Barrett/severe GERD.
Recheck CBC / ironIf presented anemicConfirm the anemia corrects — failure to correct suggests ongoing loss → re-scope.
The most-missed follow-up step in PUD is the test-of-cure. Order it at the eradication visit so it actually happens — and remind the patient to hold the PPI beforehand or the result is worthless.
Fundic gland polyps — a benign but common finding on long-term PPI therapy. A visual reminder to use the lowest effective dose and deprescribe once the ulcer cause is fixed.

Prevent

Prevention & USPSTF

🛡️

Gastroprotection & relevant USPSTF statements

The most important prevention in PUD is choosing who needs gastroprotection before they ulcerate — high-risk NSAID/aspirin users. There is no USPSTF population screen for H. pylori or PUD (testing is disease-driven, per ACG); the USPSTF statement that most bears on PUD is the aspirin one, precisely because aspirin causes GI bleeding.

GradeRecommendationPopulation / relevance to PUD
CIndividualize low-dose aspirin for primary CVD prevention (USPSTF 2022)Adults 40–59 with ≥10% 10-yr CVD risk — small net benefit; GI bleeding risk is the limiting factor.
DDo NOT initiate aspirin for primary CVD prevention (USPSTF 2022)Adults ≥60 — bleeding harm outweighs benefit. (Does not apply to secondary prevention.)
BColorectal cancer screeningAdults 45–75 — relevant since GI symptoms/anemia overlap; not PUD-specific.

NSAID-ulcer primary prophylaxis — who gets a PPI with their NSAID

Co-prescribe a PPI (most convenient) or misoprostol 200 mcg QID when starting/continuing an NSAID in a high-risk patient: prior ulcer or ulcer bleed, age >65, high-dose NSAID, or concurrent aspirin / anticoagulant / corticosteroid / SSRI. Also test-and-treat H. pylori before long-term NSAID/aspirin. In the highest-risk (prior bleed): COX-2 selective + PPI.

Gastroprotection hierarchy matters: sucralfate and H₂-blockers are inadequate to prevent NSAID gastric ulcers (misoprostol 1.6% vs sucralfate 16% in an RCT; H₂RAs prevent duodenal but not gastric ulcers). For NSAID gastroprotection, use a PPI or misoprostol.
Smoking & alcohol: smoking impairs ulcer healing and raises recurrence/complications — counsel cessation at every visit; heavy alcohol is a mucosal irritant.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED now: hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis · melena or hematochezia · syncope/near-syncope or orthostasis · sudden severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen (perforation) · persistent vomiting with dehydration/succussion splash (gastric outlet obstruction) · symptomatic or rapidly falling hemoglobin.
Refer for prompt EGD (don't just treat empirically): any alarm feature — new dyspepsia age ≥60, weight loss, dysphagia/odynophagia, iron-deficiency anemia, GI bleeding, family history of upper-GI cancer, or a gastric ulcer that hasn't confirmed healing.
Use the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (in the Wards tab) to triage a stable patient with suspected bleeding: GBS 0–1 can often be managed as an outpatient with early endoscopy; ≥2 should be admitted.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & the Forrest ladder

Most ward admissions for PUD are for a complication — usually bleeding. Admit for:

  • Active or recent GI bleeding / high-risk endoscopic stigmata, or symptomatic anemia / transfusion need
  • Hemodynamic change — tachycardia, hypotension, or orthostasis
  • Perforation or gastric outlet obstruction
  • Inability to tolerate PO / intractable pain
  • Glasgow-Blatchford ≥2 (not an outpatient candidate) or significant comorbidity/anticoagulation

Forrest classification — the post-endoscopy number that drives everything

Once the ulcer is scoped, its Forrest class predicts rebleeding and decides who needs endoscopic hemostasis + 72 h of IV PPI vs oral PPI and early discharge.

ForrestStigma of hemorrhageRebleed (untreated)Endoscopic therapy?
IaActive spurting (arterial)~55–90%Yes — high-risk
IbActive oozing~10–27%Yes — high-risk
IIaNon-bleeding visible vessel~40–50%Yes — high-risk
IIbAdherent clot~20–30%Consider (remove clot ± treat)
IIcFlat pigmented spot~7–10%No — oral PPI
IIIClean ulcer base~3–5%No — early feed/discharge
Ia/Ib/IIa (and often IIb) = "high-risk stigmata" → endoscopic hemostasis + 72 h IV high-dose PPI + inpatient observation. IIc/III = low-risk → oral PPI, early feeding, and often early discharge.

The Hb rows are sex-specific (men score at <13, women at <12); this simplified selector rounds the middle band — for a precise value use MDCalc GBS. Point values: Blatchford 2000 / ACG 2021.
🧮

AIMS65 — in-hospital mortality

Five equally-weighted bedside variables (1 point each). Fast; predicts in-hospital mortality and the need for higher-level care.

Albumin <3.0 g/dL +1
INR >1.5 +1
Altered mental status (GCS <14) +1
Systolic BP ≤90 mmHg +1
Age ≥65 years +1
0
Mortality by score (validation): 0 ≈ 0.3% · 1 ≈ 1% · 2 ≈ 3% · 3 ≈ 9% · 4 ≈ 15% · 5 ≈ 25% (AIMS65 validation, AJG 2015). Score ≥2 → consider monitored/step-down care. For post-endoscopic rebleeding/mortality use the full Rockall score (MDCalc) — its continuous point tables are best used from the validated source.

Treat

Acute bleeding management

💊

UGI-bleed ladder — resuscitate → PPI → scope

1
Resuscitate & transfuse (restrictively)
Blood/volume first — the scope can wait until they're stable.
▾
Over-transfusion raises venous/portal pressure and re-opens clot. Villanueva 2013: a restrictive strategy improved 6-week survival (95% vs 91%) with less rebleeding.
  • Transfuse RBCs at Hb <7 g/dL, target 7–9 (hemodynamically stable, non-exsanguinating).
  • Use a higher threshold (~<8) in ACS/unstable CAD; during massive active bleeding, transfuse to clinical response, don't chase a number.
  • Transfuse platelets if <50k with active bleeding; correct clinically significant coagulopathy — but don't delay the scope for a mild INR.
2
IV PPI — pre- and post-endoscopy
Stabilize clot at pH >6; downstage stigmata.
▾
Clot is chemically fragile in acid (pepsin lyses it; platelets/fibrin fail below pH ~6). PPIs raise pH to stabilize clot — but they do not stop arterial spurting; that needs the scope.
PhaseRegimenEvidence / note
Pre-endoscopy (optional)Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr infusionLau 2007: less active bleeding at scope (6% vs 15%), less endoscopic therapy needed. Never delay the scope for it.
Post-endoscopy, high-risk (Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa) — 72 hContinuous 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hr OR intermittent 80 mg → 40 mg IV/PO BID–TIDLau 2000: rebleeding 6.7% vs 22.5%. Intermittent is non-inferior to continuous — simpler and cheaper.
After 72 hStep down to oral PPI; high-risk ulcers → PPI BID through day 14, then daily to complete 4–8 wkThen treat the cause (eradicate H. pylori, stop NSAID).
Prokinetic: give erythromycin 250 mg IV (~3 mg/kg) 30–90 min before EGD (motilin agonist) to clear blood/clot and improve the view — check the QT first.
3
Endoscopy & endoscopic hemostasis
Within 24 h — diagnostic + therapeutic.
▾
  • Timing: within 24 h of presentation after resuscitation. Lau 2020: urgent (<6 h) endoscopy did not beat early (≤24 h) — 30-day mortality 8.9% vs 6.6%. Resuscitate first.
  • Treat Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa (± IIb after clot removal). Modalities: through-the-scope clips, thermal (bipolar/heater probe), or injection.
  • Never use epinephrine injection alone — combine with a second modality (clip or thermal). OTSC or TC-325 powder for refractory/diffuse bleeding.
  • Test for H. pylori (biopsy at index EGD); acute bleeding lowers sensitivity, so a negative test must be repeated as an outpatient.
Do NOT give tranexamic acid for the bleeding (HALT-IT 2020 — no mortality benefit, more VTE and seizures).
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

TrendCadenceWhat it tells you
Hemoglobinq6–12 h while active, then dailyA drop >2 g/dL or below the transfusion threshold suggests ongoing/recurrent bleeding.
Vitals / orthostaticsContinuous–q4 hTachycardia and a rising shock index are early rebleeding signs before Hb falls.
BUNDailyA falling BUN suggests the bleeding has stopped (no new protein meal in the gut).
Rebleeding signsEvery shiftFresh hematemesis/melena, new tachycardia/hypotension, Hb drop → repeat endoscopy.
Diet advancePer Forrest classLow-risk (IIc/III) → early feeding; high-risk → advance after the 72-h high-risk window.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU/step-down for any of:
  • SBP <90 mmHg or shock index >1 despite resuscitation
  • Ongoing/rising transfusion requirement (e.g., >2–4 units to hold Hb)
  • Rebleeding after endoscopic therapy
  • Active hematemesis with airway/aspiration risk or altered mental status
  • Need for vasopressors, a rising lactate, or perforation with sepsis physiology
A first rebleed after endoscopy is usually managed by repeat endoscopy — but the patient belongs in a monitored bed while that's arranged.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: hemostasis achieved (low-risk stigmata, or high-risk successfully treated after ~72 h observation) · hemodynamically stable · stable Hb ×24 h without ongoing transfusion · tolerating diet + oral PPI · H. pylori/NSAID plan documented · antiplatelet/anticoagulant restart plan set.

Resume low-dose aspirin early (typically within 3–7 days once hemostasis is secure) if it's for secondary CV prevention — Sung 2010: continuing slightly raised rebleeding but markedly lowered all-cause/CV mortality. Continue PPI co-therapy. Restart anticoagulation within days–1 week, individualized to thrombotic risk.

Home

Most patients: hemostasis secure, stable Hb, tolerating PO, reliable follow-up for test-of-cure.

Home health

Stable but needs nursing for IV meds, wound, or frailty support; anemia monitoring at home.

SNF

Deconditioned/elderly needing 24 h skilled nursing & supervision before independent living.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely needed for uncomplicated PUD; consider after prolonged ICU/surgery deconditioning.

LTAC

Prolonged complex recovery (e.g., post-surgical, ventilator weaning).

Hospice / palliative

Bleeding from incurable malignancy, or goals-of-care favoring comfort.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

ICU for PUD means one of three things: massive hemorrhage / hemorrhagic shock · rebleeding after endoscopic hemostasis · perforation with peritonitis/sepsis.
  • Massive hematemesis or hemorrhagic shock (SBP <90, shock index >1) despite resuscitation
  • Ongoing transfusion requirement or rebleeding after endoscopic therapy
  • Airway compromise — active hematemesis + altered mental status → intubate
  • Need for vasopressors, massive transfusion, IR embolization, or surgery
  • Perforation (pneumoperitoneum + peritonitis) → resuscitate, antibiotics, urgent surgery
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, transfusion, targets

  • Access: two large-bore peripheral IVs (14–16 g) — short & wide beats a long central line for rapid transfusion — ± central venous access; arterial line for continuous BP in shock.
  • Massive Transfusion Protocol for uncontrolled hemorrhage → balanced RBC : FFP : platelets ≈ 1:1:1. Monitor ionized calcium (citrate chelation → hypocalcemia), K⁺, and temperature; avoid the lethal triad (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy). Use TEG/ROTEM where available.
  • Once controlled, return to the restrictive Hb <7 threshold.
  • Airway: intubate before endoscopy for massive hematemesis, altered mental status, or high aspiration risk.
In brisk exsanguinating bleeding the initial Hb lags — you lose whole blood, so the concentration looks normal until fluids dilute it. Resuscitate to the patient (perfusion, lactate, urine output), not the first Hb value.
Support

Pressors & reversal

💉

Vasopressors — a bridge, not a substitute for blood

Hemorrhagic shock is a volume problem — the definitive treatments are blood + hemostasis. Pressors only buy time by squeezing an underfilled tank; leaning on them instead of transfusing worsens perfusion. Start one only when MAP stays low despite adequate volume/blood while you get to the source.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ > β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ SVR, mild ↑ COFirst-line bridge for shock persisting despite resuscitation
VasopressinV₁ receptor0.03 units/min (fixed)↑ SVR (catecholamine-sparing)Add-on when norepinephrine alone insufficient
Epinephrineβ₁ = α₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ CO + ↑ SVRRefractory shock / peri-arrest
🧯

Reversal of anticoagulation (life-threatening bleed)

Agent on boardReversalNotes
WarfarinVitamin K 10 mg IV (slow) + 4-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg, or fixed ~1500 u for non-ICH major bleed)PCC is faster/lower-volume than FFP; vitamin K sustains reversal.
DabigatranIdarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g boluses)Specific antidote; near-immediate.
Apixaban / rivaroxabanAndexanet alfa (dose by agent/timing), or 4F-PCC 50 units/kg if unavailableFactor Xa inhibitors.
HeparinProtamine 1 mg per 100 units (max 50 mg)Partial reversal for LMWH.
AntiplateletsHold the agent; platelet transfusion generally not helpful for reversalWeigh cardiac/stent risk before stopping; avoid reflexive platelets.
Airway

Airway protection

🌬️

Intubate before the scope when the airway is at risk

The ventilator is rarely the point in PUD — airway protection is. Aspiration of blood/gastric contents is a real killer during massive hematemesis and endoscopy.

Intubate before endoscopy for: massive/ongoing hematemesis · altered mental status (can't protect the airway) · agitation precluding a safe scope · hemodynamic instability with high aspiration risk. Use a rapid-sequence approach with suction ready; expect hypotension → resuscitate first.

Once intubated, default to lung-protective settings (there's no PUD-specific ventilation) and wean as the bleeding is controlled:

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective
PEEP
5–8
titrate to oxygenation
FiO₂
100%→wean
SpO₂ 92–96%
Free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) on a supine film — a perforated viscus until proven otherwise. A perforated ulcer is a classic cause and a surgical emergency.

Rescue

Refractory bleeding, perforation & SUP

⚙️

When endoscopy isn't enough — the rescue ladder

1
Repeat endoscopy
First move for a first rebleed.
▾

A first rebleed after successful hemostasis is usually managed by repeat endoscopy (often succeeds; add an OTSC or a second modality). Routine "second-look" endoscopy is not recommended — scope again for clinical rebleeding.

2
Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE)
IR — the preferred rescue after failed endoscopy.
▾
Angiographic embolization occludes the culprit vessel without a laparotomy — e.g., gastroduodenal artery embolization for a posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the GDA. CT angiography can localize (needs ~0.3–0.5 mL/min active extravasation).

TAE before surgery is the modern preference in most centers (Barkun 2019).

3
Surgery
When endoscopy + IR fail, or for perforation.
▾
  • Refractory bleeding: oversew/ligate the vessel (duodenotomy with GDA ligation for a posterior DU), ± vagotomy in rare acid-hypersecretory cases.
  • Perforation (pneumoperitoneum + peritonitis): resuscitation + broad-spectrum antibiotics + IV PPI + urgent surgery. Standard repair = Graham (omental) patch — vascularized omentum sutured over the perforation (open or laparoscopic). Nonoperative management only for selected contained/sealed perforations in stable patients.

Gastric outlet obstruction (GOO)

Chronic peri-pyloric/duodenal ulcers → edema + scarring → vomiting, early satiety, weight loss, succussion splash, and a hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Manage with NG decompression, IV fluids/electrolyte correction, IV PPI, EGD to exclude malignancy → endoscopic balloon dilation for benign strictures; surgery (gastrojejunostomy/pyloroplasty) if refractory. Treat the underlying H. pylori/NSAID cause.

🛡️

Stress-ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) — a distinct ICU question

Distinct from treating a known ulcer: SUP prevents stress-related mucosal bleeding in critically ill patients whose splanchnic perfusion is compromised.

Who qualifies (highest yield): mechanical ventilation >48 h and coagulopathy (platelets <50k, INR >1.5, or PTT >2× control) are the two strongest risk factors (Cook 1994). The 2024 ASHP/SCCM guideline also flags shock and chronic liver disease. PPI or H₂RA (IV or oral) are both acceptable.
REVISE 2024 (NEJM): in invasively ventilated patients, pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily cut clinically important UGI bleeding to 1.0% vs 3.5% (no mortality difference, no pneumonia/C. diff signal) — supports PPI prophylaxis in ventilated ICU patients. Deprescribe once risk factors resolve / enteral feeding is tolerated.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down to the ward when ALL of:
  • Hemostasis achieved and no rebleeding
  • Off vasopressors and no ongoing transfusion requirement
  • Stable serial hemoglobin ×24–48 h
  • Resolving lactate; extubated / protecting the airway
  • Perforation/sepsis physiology resolving
Not yet if: any fresh hematemesis/melena, a Hb drop needing transfusion in the last 24 h, a pressor requirement, or a high-risk ulcer still inside its 72-h window with borderline hemodynamics.
